problem: Frontier-based SLAM and exploration keep a single global map, so memory and the cost of subgoal search grow rapidly with environment size. Prior submap SLAM splits space periodically or randomly rather than by properties of the space, and grid-cell fragmentation models had not been used functionally for mapping.
motivation: Animals explore large spaces efficiently, and grid cell maps fragment at doorways and sharp turns, which can be modeled as surprisal-based online clustering. The authors reason that several simple local models, with boundaries placed where the local model stops predicting well, could give cheaper exploration and natural subgoals.
key_idea: Build local predictive maps and fragment them when z-scored surprisal exceeds a threshold. Store fragments in long-term memory as a connectivity graph, recall them at fracture points, and use fracture points as subgoals for hierarchical exploration.
insight: Surprisal-driven fragmentation yields better coverage-per-memory and coverage-per-time than random or uniform fragmentation at similar fragmentation rates. In the Random/Uniform ablation, for example, Random P=0.005 reaches 49.1 coverage at 30.5 memory, versus FARMap at 56.6 and 31.4. The benefit grows with environment size because the agent plans only on a small local map (about 4x faster in large environments). The z-score threshold and the LTM subgoal both add coverage at a modest memory and time cost, and the threshold ρ trades fragment count against memory.
method: Local predictive map (STM): a decaying trace of egocentric observations, M_t = γ·M_{t-1} + (1-γ)·o'_t, on a map that grows with exploration; the observation is rotated and zero-padded into map coordinates.

Surprisal: s_t = 1 - c_t, where c_t is the average similarity between the visible observation and the pre-update local map; it is z-scored against a running mean and std per map (at least 25 samples before fragmentation is allowed).

Fragmentation: when z_t > ρ (=2), the current map is stored in LTM together with its frontier/known ratio q_c and the fracture point, and a new empty local map is started. A fracture border prevents over-fragmentation.

Recall: when the agent crosses a fracture point or border, the current map is stored and the adjacent stored map is loaded into STM; LTM holds a connectivity graph whose nodes are fragments and whose edges are shared fracture points.

Subgoal selection: within a fragment, frontier-edges are sampled with weight |F|·1(not behind agent)/d. Across fragments, g = argmax q_i/(d_{i,c}+ε) picks the least-explored nearby fragment, and the fracture point toward it becomes the subgoal.
Planner: Dijkstra on the local map (RRT tested as an alternative), with the agent updating the map and checking fragmentation continuously while moving.
Procedural environment generator: connects, merges and boundary-flips grid-patterned rooms into 1,500 maps (small, medium, large), plus 345 dynamic maps whose wall colors change every step.

setting.backbone: Classical algorithm (Frontier exploration + surprisal-based fragmentation, Dijkstra planner); no learned model in the main method. Neural SLAM (pre-trained) is used in one extension.
setting.observation: egocentric top-down 15x15 view with 130° FOV and occlusion (procedural grids); 360° laser scan (ROS/Gazebo); RGB via Neural SLAM (Gibson/Habitat)
setting.action_space: discrete grid moves via Dijkstra path to subgoals; continuous TurtleBot3 navigation via move_base in ROS
setting.simulator: Custom procedural grid environments; ROS/Gazebo; Habitat (Gibson) for the Neural SLAM experiment
setting.privileged: none (agent position and heading are assumed known)

numbers_note: No standard VLN or ObjectNav benchmarks are used. The ROS/Gazebo results (Table 4, four environments, coverage/memory in thousands of cells) are omitted from the numbers list; the main procedural results are reported only as means with bootstrap CIs.
results: On 1,500 procedural environments FARMap beats the Frontier baseline in coverage, memory and wall-clock time, with the gap widening as environments grow. In large environments it reaches 56.6% coverage versus 41.4%, at 31.4% memory versus 44.4% and 352.5 s versus 1261 s (about 4x faster). It also gives better coverage with less memory in most ROS environments and improves Neural SLAM coverage (0.833 vs 0.818). Its fracture points align with grid-cell remapping locations in simulated rat experiments.
limitations: Evaluated only on 2D maps in simulation (procedural grids, Gazebo, one Gibson scene) with no real robot, and it is a proof of concept built on Frontier exploration.

Assumes accurate agent pose, and LTM lives in external memory whose retrieval cost matters on slow storage; the fragmentation threshold ρ must be tuned, and the ROS results are mixed (e.g. more memory in AWS Office, equal coverage in Environment 2).
Confidence intervals are very wide because of aggregation over heterogeneous environments; the neuroscience comparison is only qualitative.
